strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: dense pretrained models fail dramatically when sparsified to dilated attention patterns at inference time, and the paper provides clear empirical evidence and diagnosis (disconnected receptive field) for this failure across both training-from-scratch and inference-time sparsification settings.

The proposed RAT+ architecture (overlapped/full-sequence recurrence + active recurrence learning via joint dense/sparse training) is a natural but non-trivial extension of RAT, and the paper carefully motivates each design choice with targeted ablations (Table 3, Table 7, Fig. 6, Fig. 8) that isolate the contribution of overlapped chunking and active recurrence learning.

Extensive empirical validation across model scales (1.5B and 2.6B parameters, 100B-200B tokens), multiple benchmark families (commonsense reasoning, LongBench, RULER/NIAH), and multiple sparsification schemes (dilated, dilated+local, layer/head hybrids, top-k block attention with two block-selection variants), lending reasonably broad support to the central claims.

Interesting and somewhat novel secondary finding that recurrence-augmented representations also improve top-k block attention (not just dilated attention), with a plausible mechanistic hypothesis (better block-level content aggregation for scoring) and supporting NIAH evidence.

Thorough efficiency characterization (prefilling and decoding latency, end-to-end throughput) across hidden dimensions and context lengths, demonstrating that claimed speedups are realizable in practice (e.g., substantial decoding throughput gains at large context lengths), which strengthens the practical significance of the contribution.

Reasonably transparent reporting of limitations of the hybrid design space (explicitly stated as a feasibility demonstration rather than an optimality claim) and honest discussion of where the method underperforms (e.g., RepoBench-P favoring local attention, some NIAH subtasks degrading substantially at high dilation).
weaknesses: Model scale (1.5B/2.6B parameters, 100-200B tokens) is modest relative to current LLM practice; while the paper shows the dense-sparse gap shrinks with scale (Fig. 5), it remains unclear whether the method's benefits and the underlying failure mode persist at scales more representative of deployed models, and this extrapolation is only lightly supported.

The comparisons are largely against internal ablations (dense attention baselines, RAT trained from scratch) rather than against a broader set of contemporary inference-time sparsification or hybrid-architecture baselines (e.g., DuoAttention, MInference, SnapKV, H2O), making it harder to contextualize how RAT+ compares to the current state of the art in absolute terms.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported anywhere (perplexity, downstream accuracy, or efficiency numbers), which is a concern given that some reported differences (e.g., 1-2 point accuracy gaps) are fairly small.

The hybrid layer-wise/head-wise sparsification results are explicitly presented as "feasibility" demonstrations rather than competitive configurations, and in the reported examples do not outperform the plain dilated pattern on average, somewhat undercutting the paper's framing of flexible hybrid inference as a key advantage.

The extra parameters/FLOPs introduced by the additional recurrence projection are not quantitatively analyzed or compared against baselines under strictly matched parameter budgets in most tables (the paper explicitly defers this to future work), leaving some ambiguity about whether reported gains are partly attributable to extra capacity rather than the architectural mechanism alone.

The empirical choice of L*=64 lacks a principled derivation and is justified purely via an empirical sweep (Fig. 6); the paper does not offer theoretical insight into why this particular length is a good general trade-off across tasks/domains, limiting the generality of this design decision.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy (D, D†, L, L*, W, K, etc.), and the explanation of some phenomena (e.g., recurrence output covariate shift in Fig. 8) is somewhat informal/hand-wavy rather than rigorously characterized, which may hinder reproducibility and clarity for readers less familiar with the RAT lineage.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: enabling a single densely-pretrained model to be flexibly sparsified into dilated attention patterns at inference time without per-configuration retraining, in contrast to prior training-from-scratch (RAT) or naive inference-time sparsification approaches that fail for dilation.

The proposed techniques (full-sequence recurrence with overlapped chunking, and active recurrence learning via joint dense/sparse training) are grounded in careful diagnostic analyses (Sec. 3, Table 1, Table 2, Fig. 9) that convincingly motivate each design choice rather than being purely ad hoc.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple model scales (1.5B, 2.6B, 7.6B parameters) and token budgets (100B-200B), with consistent trends showing that the dense-sparse performance gap shrinks with scale, supporting the scalability claim.
Broad set of ablations (chunk overlap, active recurrence learning, hierarchical recurrence placement, NoPE, multi-dilation adaptation, choice of L=64) that isolate the contribution of each component.

Thorough efficiency characterization (prefilling/decoding latency, KV cache, end-to-end throughput) across hidden sizes and context lengths, showing large and plausible speedups (up to tens of x) that are consistent with the theoretical FLOPs/KV cache reduction.

Additional finding that recurrence also improves top-k block attention (orthogonal sparsity pattern) broadens the significance of the contribution beyond dilation alone, and is supported by head-level hit-rate analysis (Table 9).

Reasonably detailed implementation/hyperparameter documentation in the appendix supports reproducibility, and comparisons against relevant baselines (GQA/MQA, SSMs, StreamingLLM, Quest, MoBA, SnapKV) help position the method.
weaknesses: Downstream accuracy numbers, especially on LongBench, are quite low in absolute terms (teens to low twenties), and the paper itself notes pretrained-only models can be sensitive to prompt format; this makes some comparative claims (e.g., about hybrid patterns or dilation vs. local attention) harder to trust as robust rather than noise-driven.

The method still requires a 1B-token 'resolution adaptation' stage per (or jointly per multiple) dilation configuration, which, while much cheaper than full retraining, means the claimed 'infer sparse' flexibility is not fully training-free; the degree of overhead this adds relative to alternative approaches is not deeply quantified in wall-clock/cost terms.

The search over hybrid layer/head sparsity configurations is explicitly left unexplored ("demonstrate feasibility rather than optimality"), so a key practical use-case (finding good hybrid configs) is not actually solved, limiting the immediate practical utility of that contribution.

Some comparisons may be confounded by implementation differences (e.g., the paper notes it does not use RAT's parameter-sharing scheme for attention projections, unlike the original RAT), which could affect the fairness of RAT vs. RAT+ comparisons.

Efficiency numbers rely on generic PyTorch associative scan and FlexAttention rather than dedicated fused CUDA kernels, which the authors acknowledge could change practical speedups; current numbers may not reflect achievable production performance.

The choice of the active recurrence length L*=64 remains a largely empirical hyperparameter with limited theoretical justification beyond a single trade-off plot (Fig. 7), and it is unclear how this choice would generalize to substantially different context lengths or domains (e.g., code, multilingual).

No comparison at matched large token budgets against a true dilated-attention-from-scratch model at the 7B scale, so it is not fully clear how much of the closing dense/sparse gap at scale is inherent to increasing model capacity versus specific to the RAT+ design.
Presentation has minor issues (a few typos, dense notation-heavy exposition) that could be polished for clarity.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: Table 1 and Table 2 convincingly demonstrate both that recurrence is necessary for dilated attention to train well from scratch, and that naive inference-time sparsification of dense attention into dilated patterns fails badly (perplexity explodes to >100 at D=64), justifying the need for a new architecture.

The two proposed techniques (full-sequence/overlapped recurrence and active recurrence learning via joint dense/sparse training) are simple, well-motivated by careful diagnostic analysis (e.g., distribution shift at initial recurrence steps in Fig. 9, lazy recurrence learning under naive joint training), and clearly ablated (Table 12, Fig. 7) to isolate their individual contributions.

Strong scale of empirical validation: experiments span 1.5B/2.6B/7.6B parameter models trained on up to 200B tokens, which is unusually substantial for an architecture paper and increases confidence that the findings generalize beyond a toy setting; the observation that the dense-sparse gap shrinks with scale (Fig. 6) is a valuable and non-trivial finding.

Comprehensive efficiency characterization (Figs. 2 and 4, extensive latency tables in the appendix) covering both prefilling and decoding across hidden dimensions and context lengths, giving a realistic picture of wall-clock speedups rather than relying solely on FLOPs/KV cache counting.

Thoughtful positioning against a wide range of alternative efficiency methods (GQA/MQA, SSMs, StreamingLLM, Quest, MoBA, SnapKV), with apples-to-apples comparisons (e.g., matched training FLOPs for GQA/MQA in Fig. 5) and an interesting additional finding that RAT+'s recurrence also improves top-k block attention scoring (Fig. 3, Table 9), broadening the contribution's relevance.

Reasonably transparent limitations and future-work discussion (e.g., acknowledging hybrid pattern search is not optimized, CUDA kernel optimization is left to future work, and code repository link is provided though not filled in the given draft).
weaknesses: Absolute LongBench performance is quite low across all configurations (e.g., mostly teens on NarrativeQA, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA in Table 5) and the paper itself flags that pretrained-only model evaluation on prompt-heavy LongBench tasks is unreliable, which weakens confidence in the long-context claims relative to the cleaner commonsense-reasoning and NIAH results.

The core architectural idea builds incrementally on the existing RAT architecture (recurrence + dilated attention), and the novelty largely resides in two relatively simple training-recipe modifications (full-sequence recurrence, joint dense/sparse training) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; this is a valid but modest degree of originality.

The choice of L*=64 as the active recurrence length is empirically tuned via a single ablation sweep (Fig. 7) without deeper theoretical justification, and it is unclear how this hyperparameter should be selected for different model scales, data domains, or context lengths beyond the ones tested.

The hybrid layer/head sparsification patterns are presented only as feasibility demonstrations rather than being systematically optimized or evaluated, so the practical value of this claimed flexibility (a key selling point of the paper) remains under-explored.

Code availability is stated but the actual link is missing in the manuscript, and some implementation details (e.g., precise recurrence gating parameterization, projection sharing choices) are described somewhat tersely in the appendix, which could hinder exact reproducibility.

Reported speedups and comparisons with top-k block attention baselines (Quest/MoBA) depend heavily on block-size choices that are shown to be very sensitive (Table 7), and the paper's chosen operating points for comparison could be seen as favorable to RAT+ without a fully systematic sweep over baseline hyperparameters.
